questions.q: How does GRANT SELECT from Lesson 42 differ from row/column-level security?
options: GRANT SELECT already provides row-level filtering automatically
Row/column security replaces the need for GRANT SELECT entirely
GRANT SELECT is all-or-nothing for a whole table; row/column-level security allows finer control over specific rows or column values
They are functionally identical, just with different syntax
questions.explain: Real governance often needs finer control than whole-table access alone provides.

questions.q: What does a column mask do?
options: A function applied automatically on every query, replacing a column's real value with something else (like 'REDACTED') for certain users
It creates a physical copy of the table with the column removed
It permanently deletes a column from the table
It only works on numeric columns, never strings
questions.explain: is_member() checks the querying user's group membership at query time — nothing about the query itself changes.

questions.q: How does a row filter differ from a column mask?
options: A row filter and column mask do exactly the same thing
Row filters replace GRANT SELECT entirely
Row filters can only be applied to managed tables, never external ones
A row filter returns true/false per row, hiding entire rows that evaluate to false, rather than masking a specific column's value
questions.explain: An admin group member might see every row, while everyone else sees only rows matching their own region.

questions.q: Do column masks and row filters create separate copies of data for different users?
options: Yes, but only for row filters, not column masks
Yes, a separate physical copy is created per user group
It depends on whether the table is managed or external
No — there's still exactly one table, with masking/filtering functions evaluated fresh on every query based on who's asking
questions.explain: This is genuinely different from maintaining separate tables per audience, which would mean running the whole pipeline multiple times.

questions.q: Why is applying a row filter to one table preferable to maintaining separate tables per audience?
options: There's no real benefit; both approaches are equally practical
Row filters are required by Delta Lake's file format
It avoids running Chapter 3's entire medallion pipeline multiple times just to produce different audience-specific copies
Separate tables are always faster to query than a single filtered table
questions.explain: A single source of truth with per-query filtering avoids the overhead and drift risk of maintaining multiple copies.
